questions.q: In basic cluster anatomy, what is a 'node'?
options: A single machine in the cluster with its own CPU, memory, and often GPU resources
A single python script submitted to the scheduler
The queue that holds pending work
A synonym for the scheduler itself
questions.explain: A cluster is a pool of nodes -- individual machines each with their own compute resources -- managed collectively by a scheduler.

questions.q: What does the scheduler actually need to know about a submitted job?
options: The full source code logic of what the job does internally
What resources it requested (GPUs, memory, time) and when it's done -- not what the code itself does
Only the researcher's name who submitted it
The git commit hash the job was built from
questions.explain: The scheduler's job is resource allocation: it cares about the resource request in a job script (like #SBATCH directives) and the job's running/completed state, not the semantics of the code being executed.

questions.q: What does it usually mean when a submitted job stays in the 'pending' state for a long time?
options: The cluster's scheduler has crashed
The job's code has a bug and will never run
The requested resources (e.g. a specific GPU type, a large memory request) aren't currently available
The job has already completed successfully
questions.explain: A job stuck pending typically means the scheduler hasn't yet found a node with the requested resources free -- it's a resource-availability issue, not necessarily an error.

questions.q: What is the main difference between a batch job and an interactive job?
options: Batch jobs always use more GPUs than interactive jobs
Interactive jobs run unattended, while batch jobs hold open a live terminal session
Batch jobs run unattended once submitted; interactive jobs hold open a terminal session on an allocated node for live debugging
There is no practical difference; both terms describe the same thing
questions.explain: Batch jobs are submit-and-walk-away; interactive jobs (e.g. via srun --pty bash in Slurm) keep a live shell open on an allocated node, typically used for debugging before committing to a long unattended run.

questions.q: Which Slurm command lets a researcher check the current state of their own submitted jobs?
options: sbatch -u $USER
squeue -u $USER
srun --list
kubectl get pods
questions.explain: squeue -u $USER lists a user's jobs and their current state (pending, running, etc.) in Slurm. kubectl get pods is the Kubernetes equivalent, not a Slurm command.
